quick.summary: Why your layout review gets stuck on colors, and how to fix it.
quick.takeaway: Set the stage. Get them to agree on the problem before showing the design.

parts.title: Set the stage first

beats.line: I showed a beautiful layout. They argued about button colors for twenty minutes. Why?
Imagine a doctor handing you a pill before telling you what is wrong.
I would not take it. I want to know the diagnosis first.
Right. Your room had no shared context.
Can I just say they lacked the background?
Much better. You showed the solution before they understood the problem.
So I need to set the stage first. Start with the user pain.
Yes. Get them to agree on the problem before showing any pictures.
But what if they still interrupt me while I set the stage?

parts.cliff: How to pause the early interruptions.

beats.line: When they interrupt early, they are usually trying to solve the problem.
True. They jump straight to ideas.
Use a kitchen rule. A chef tells the kitchen what is on the menu.
So I tell them how the meeting will run?
Yes. Give them a map. Tell them when to listen and when to speak.

board.text: tell them how it will run

beats.line: I will show the problem for five minutes. Hold your ideas until then.
Perfect. You gave them a job for later.
Then I show the design, and ask for their ideas?
Yes. Now they are ready to help you cook.

quiz.question: Why do meetings often get stuck on small design details?
options: The team does not agree on the problem yet.
The colors are not trendy enough.
The meeting was scheduled too early.
quiz.explanation: If people do not understand the underlying problem, they will focus on whatever visual details they can see.

quiz.question: You should tell the room how the meeting will run before showing designs.
quiz.explanation: Telling people when to listen and when to speak stops early interruptions.
